title: The Real Story in Maine
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek, a former 1:1 iPad program architect, responds to Jared Cooney Horvath's widely shared 'digital delusion' argument about Maine's laptop initiative by challenging its causal reasoning rather than defending edtech uncritically. He agrees that technology never delivered the promised revolution, but faults schools for leading with devices instead of pedagogy, not the devices themselves, and shows that Horvath's own comparison collapses once confounding variables are accounted for: Massachusetts's NAEP rise traces to a 1993 funding and accountability overhaul that predates its laptop program by a decade, while Maine spent the same decades absorbing rural consolidation, a repealed diploma law, and teacher shortages. Marcinek turns Horvath's cited effect size, a small positive 0.12 to 0.16 from a meta-analysis, into evidence against the 'rip it all out' conclusion, arguing a modest positive effect supports his own thesis that the teacher and pedagogy, not the device, is the real intervention. He extends the same skepticism to smartphone bans, citing the University of Birmingham's Lancet-published SMART Schools study of 1,227 students across 30 schools, which found no wellbeing or attainment differences between ban and non-ban schools, and argues that consumer smartphones parents hand children at nine or ten are being wrongly conflated with managed school devices used for instruction.
points: Marcinek's core methodological critique is that Horvath's own piece admits twice that 'the data proves nothing' about laptops harming learning, yet still lets correlation do persuasive work, a move Marcinek calls 'a chart with a vibe' rather than analysis.

He isolates the confound that undermines the Maine-versus-Massachusetts comparison: Massachusetts's NAEP gains trace to the 1993 Education Reform Act's funding and MCAS accountability system, a full decade before its laptop program (MLTI) even existed.

He reinterprets the Zheng meta-analysis's own reported effect size (+0.12 to +0.16 for 1:1 programs) as evidence for his position, small and positive, not harmful, arguing this contradicts the 'rip it all out' conclusion critics draw from the same data.

The University of Birmingham SMART Schools study (Lancet Regional Health, Europe, 2025) is cited as the first study of its kind on phone bans specifically, finding no measurable difference in wellbeing, sleep, or attainment between ban and non-ban schools across 1,227 students.

Marcinek draws a sharp distinction schools policy debates often blur: consumer smartphones handed to children by parents outside school control versus managed, purpose-built instructional devices, arguing that treating them as the same technology is 'either careless or deliberate' bad research.
quotes: That was our fault. Not the devices. Ours. We led with platforms instead of purpose. We bought first and asked pedagogical questions later.

He admits, twice, that the data proves nothing. "Is this proof that laptops harmed learning? Of course not." ... Then he waves all of that away in a single paragraph and lets the correlation do the persuading anyway. That's not analysis. That's a chart with a vibe.

Massachusetts passed the Education Reform Act in 1993, massive funding increases, curriculum frameworks, MCAS accountability, a full decade before MLTI existed. Its rise to the top of NAEP is one of the most studied policy stories in American education, and laptops have nothing to do with it.

The research literature he references, including the Zheng meta-analysis he links, finds 1:1 programs produce small positive effects, around +0.12 to +0.16. Small. Positive. Not transformational, and not harmful.

The first study of its kind, the SMART Schools study out of the University of Birmingham, published in The Lancet Regional Health, Europe (2025), compared 1,227 students across 30 schools and found no difference in mental wellbeing, anxiety, depression, sleep, physical activity, or academic attainment between schools that ban phones and schools that don't.
Conflating a consumer smartphone loaded with TikTok and a managed school device running a writing workshop is either careless or deliberate. Neither is good research.
They're doing the harder, quieter work: recalibrating, centering technology intentionally, asking "why this tool, for this learning, right now?" That's the work. It always was.
